analysis.one_liner: Extends airline pilot rest and duty-time rules to cargo flight crews.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 23 cosponsors from both parties, never left the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2012, federal rules have capped how long passenger airline pilots can work and required minimum rest between shifts, but the same rules do not apply to pilots flying all-cargo planes. This bill would have directed the Transportation Secretary to extend those duty and rest rules to cargo flight crews within 30 days. The bill went to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Cargo pilots and flight engineers gain the same limits on flight duty hours and the same minimum rest requirements as their passenger-airline counterparts, reducing the risk of flying while fatigued. People living and working under cargo flight paths also benefit indirectly, because rested crews reduce the chance of an all-cargo crash over populated areas. The bill's lead sponsor, Rep. Salud Carbajal, and its cosponsors framed it as a flight-safety fix [S2][S3][S1].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cargo flight crews and people under their flight paths

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Transportation Secretary to modify the FAA's 2012 final rule on flightcrew duty and rest requirements so that they apply to all-cargo operations in the same manner as passenger operations [S2][S3].
The change was to take effect quickly: the Secretary would have had to make the modification within 30 days of enactment, bypassing the usual notice-and-comment rulemaking process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: All-cargo air carriers would bear the cost of restructuring schedules and hiring additional crews to meet passenger-equivalent rest limits, costs that could be passed on to shippers and consumers of overnight and expedited freight. Under current rules, cargo carriers have had more scheduling flexibility because their crews were not covered by the 2012 passenger rest rule [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandate was written as a direct command to modify an existing final rule within 30 days, with the normal rulemaking requirements under 5 U.S.C. 553 waived, leaving carriers and the agency little room to tailor the rules to the different operating patterns of cargo flying, which is largely overnight work [S3].

All-cargo carriers argue that night freight schedules differ substantially from passenger operations, and an across-the-board application of the passenger rule raises their labor costs, a cost likely to show up in shipping prices and scheduling flexibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety logic is straightforward: the same human fatigue limits apply better to all flight crews than only to those carrying passengers, and the bill would have closed a gap that has existed since the 2012 rule took effect. The main cost falls on cargo carriers, who would have to hire more crews and rebuild overnight schedules, and some of that cost would reach freight customers. The bill's main design weakness was speed and rigidity rather than substance: a 30-day deadline with rulemaking procedures waived is abrupt, though the underlying requirement matched what passenger crews already live under.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, where it stayed until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the Safe Skies Act on June 23, 2021, joined by six original cosponsors including Republicans Chris Katko and Jeff Van Drew [S3][S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Aviation [S5][S1].
It ultimately gathered 23 cosponsors, 18 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but the committee never took it up and no vote was ever held in either chamber [S4][S5][S1].
When the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, the bill died; it was not reintroduced in the record provided.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: All-cargo air carriers are better off, because they continue operating under the looser scheduling flexibility of the pre-2012-rule regime, with no passenger-equivalent duty and rest limits and no added crew costs. Cargo crews remain subject to a two-tier fatigue standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: All-cargo airlines, which kept looser crew rules

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend passenger-crew rest rules to all-cargo operations [S1][S3].

for.name: 5 of 222 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsor Rep. Chris Katko [S4][S3].

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it during the 117th Congress [S5][S1].

against.name: Subcommittee on Aviation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day after introduction and held no further action on the bill [S5].

against.name: All-cargo air carriers
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in retaining the exemption from passenger-equivalent rest rules, which preserves scheduling flexibility and avoids added crew costs [S2][S3].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's cosponsorship was bipartisan from day one — 18 Democrats and 5 Republicans, with Republicans among the original cosponsors — and opposition never took the form of a recorded vote; the bill simply was never brought up [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have ended their exemption from the 2012 passenger flightcrew duty and rest rule, forcing scheduling changes and added crew costs. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against the safety interest of their crews and people under cargo flight paths.
They would gain the same duty-hour caps and minimum rest requirements as passenger crews, directly reducing fatigue risk. Their interest aligns with the general public's interest in safe skies.

They already operate under the 2012 rest rule and would be unaffected; the bill would have removed a cost disadvantage relative to cargo competitors by raising cargo carriers' compliance burden to the same standard.
